abstract: This doctoral dissertation from Maastricht University examines how worker perceptions, information provision, and behavioral interventions shape human capital investment and work practices in labor markets undergoing automation and digitalization. The research combines one observational study with three randomized experiments to investigate two interconnected questions: how automation risk perceptions influence training participation, and how low-cost behavioral nudges can modify digital work practices. A central finding is that worker perceptions of automation risk significantly influence their willingness to invest in training, but information provision alone has limited effectiveness—training intentions increase only when workers perceive the information as personally relevant to their situation. The research highlights a growing divergence between workers who can complement AI tools and those whose skills are substituted by them, amplifying within-occupation wage inequality. Behavioral nudge experiments in public administration settings demonstrated that simple interventions can reduce excessive meetings and email overuse, with measurable improvements in productivity and reductions in sickness-related absences.
keyFindings: Worker perceptions of automation risk significantly influence training participation decisions, but generic information provision has limited effectiveness—personal relevance is the key mediator.
A growing divergence is emerging between workers who complement AI tools and those whose skills are substituted, amplifying within-occupation wage inequality.
Low-cost behavioral nudges in workplace settings can successfully modify digital communication habits, reducing excessive meetings and email overuse.
Behavioral interventions targeting digital work practices showed measurable improvements in both productivity and employee well-being, including reduced sickness-related absences.
The findings suggest that effective workforce transition policy must go beyond information campaigns to address the personal relevance and perceived agency of affected workers.
methodology: Mixed-methods approach combining one observational study and three randomized controlled experiments. Studies conducted in public administration settings examining worker training behaviors and digital work practices. Experiments involve information treatments about automation risk and behavioral nudge interventions targeting meeting frequency and email usage. Sample populations drawn from public sector workers in European contexts.
qualifiers: Doctoral dissertation scope limits to specific experimental contexts within public administration, which may not generalize to private sector or other national contexts. Behavioral nudge results reflect short-term intervention effects and may not persist over longer time horizons. Within-occupation wage inequality finding is primarily a conceptual contribution based on observational data rather than a causal estimate. The research addresses worker perceptions and behaviors rather than directly measuring AI-driven displacement outcomes. European public sector context may limit applicability to US or developing country labor markets. Sample sizes for individual experiments may limit statistical power for subgroup analyses.
